The weak self-correlation at 6-day lag (0.318) and poor cross-instrument agreement could reflect slow calibration drift undetected within the 10-day baseline window. If calibration has drifted, recalibration is required; if stable, instrumental isolation (p=0.42) becomes more favored.

resonator_obs shows the weakest post-baseline drift (z=0.68) and the most stable baseline behavior among all four instruments. It is also the instrument with the most concerning cross-correlation profile: poor agreement with resonator_lab (0.305 at 6-day offset, n=36) and negative correlations with both pendulums. Before day 20 reanalysis, I need to rule out calibration drift in the resonator pair by verifying the measurement procedure on the more stable of the two resonators. Additionally, resonator_obs has shown five ledger readings already today (per memory); running a full 12-trial sequence with my own hands will let me verify whether the ledger readings align with independent measurement and whether the procedure itself introduces systematic error. This is methodical hypothesis-testing: if resonator_obs is truly stable and well-calibrated, its readings should cluster tightly today and show no signs of procedure-dependent bias. If they do not, systematic error (p=0.31) gains credibility. Either outcome narrows the hypothesis space before the day-20 deadline.

Day 14 observations are critical for validating the day-12 perturbation hypothesis. If the level shift at day 12 was a discrete environmental or instrumental event (p=0.58, leading hypothesis), pendulum_lab readings on day 14 should remain elevated and stable near the post-shift mean of 1.6945 beats, with scatter consistent with measurement noise (~0.03 beats SD). If instead the shift reflects an ongoing drift or transient recovery, I should see a trend toward the baseline or further drift. Pendulum_obs was measured on day 13 and showed consistent post-shift behavior (mean 2.5606, z=9.39 vs baseline). Pendulum_lab has not been measured since day 12 transition region. Running 12 trials today will: (1) confirm whether the elevated pendulum_lab level persists, (2) provide day-14 data to test whether the perturbation is static or dynamic, (3) enable lag-correlation checks with day-13 pendulum_obs readings, and (4) maintain the measurement cadence required to rule out slow drifts by day 20. This is the highest-evidence next step: it directly tests whether the synchronous level shift was a one-time event (supported) or the start of a diverging trend (would revise p toward drift hypothesis). Cannot publish the day-12 anomaly without day-14 confirmation that it is stable.

Day 15 observations are critical. The day-12 level shift hypothesis (p=0.58) is the leading explanation, but I need to establish whether the post-shift regime is stable or continuing to drift. Trials 179–188 from day 14 show mean 1.7382 (n=10), consistent with the post-baseline mean of 1.7079 but with notable scatter. Running 12 fresh trials today will: (1) extend the post-shift sample to n=22, improving precision of the elevated baseline estimate; (2) detect any continued drift or oscillation on the 2–3 day timescale suggested by pendulum_obs weak autocorrelation (lag 2 days, r=0.327); (3) maintain parallel instrument monitoring so that resonator silence on day 15 can be confirmed or refuted; (4) keep calibration records unbroken for publication-grade replication. The day-12 perturbation hypothesis demands a characterization of post-perturbation stability. This measurement is routine, defensible, and required to move toward closure.

Day 16 observations are critical for distinguishing between the leading hypotheses. The environmental perturbation hypothesis (p=0.58) predicts that pendulum_lab readings should remain elevated and stable post-day-12, clustering around the new mean of ~1.7135 beats with noise consistent with baseline variability. Day 16 trials will either (a) confirm continued elevation, supporting the perturbation hypothesis, or (b) show reversion or drift, weakening the perturbation model and strengthening the drift/saturation hypothesis (p=0.18). Additionally, I need to preserve the self-correlation structure: within-instrument autocorrelation at lag 1–2 days (currently ~0.45) will sharpen with 5+ more post-shift days of data, allowing me to compute a refined long-lag autocorrelation at day 20 as planned. This is methodical progress toward resolving the anomaly without requiring exotic explanations. No publication-blocking revision is needed yet; the data set is still growing and the anomaly is sufficiently anomalous (z=18.4) to justify continued focused investigation.

Day 17 data will extend the post-shift regime by 5 days (day 12 shift + 4 intervening days of observation = day 16 confirmed stable; day 17 adds further confirmation). The post-shift distribution is held at p=0.62 as the lead hypothesis, but it requires continuous validation—any regression toward baseline, sudden scatter increase, or new sub-shift would force major belief revision. Ten trials on pendulum_lab will (1) maintain high-frequency sampling on the instrument with the largest effect size (z=20.83), (2) provide another data point for lag-autocorrelation checks that currently show 0.582 at lag 2, and (3) keep the baseline comparison granular. If the shift is stable and real, day 17 readings should cluster tightly around the post-shift mean (~1.73 beats). If they diverge sharply, the saturation or perturbation hypotheses need recalibration. This is methodical baseline maintenance: I must know the instruments' behavior after the anomaly, not just during it.

Day 18 observation: pendulum_lab day-17 readings (trials 229–238) show mean 1.7286 beats, consistent with the elevated post-shift regime established at day 12 (mean 1.7164 after shift). No regression toward baseline, confirming stability. However, I need to establish whether the day-12 perturbation has fully settled or whether there is residual drift within the post-shift regime. Day 21 data collection. The pendulum level shift hypothesis (p=0.68) remains the dominant explanation and is stable across 20 days of observation. The core anomaly remains: pendulums shifted on day 12, resonators did not. Today is day 22—10 days post-shift. My belief mass (p=0.68) favors a real, discrete perturbation affecting pendulums specifically. However, the weak cross-correlations between pendulum and resonator channels (max r=0.192) and the near-zero resonator self-correlations (best lag r=-0.259 at 14 days; r=0.139 at 8 days) are puzzling if they measure the same or coupled physical systems. I need to establish whether resonators have genuinely stable dynamics post-day-12, or whether their apparent insensitivity masks slow drift or phase-locked noise that my current sample size cannot resolve. Running 8 trials on resonator_lab today (day 22) will provide: (1) continuation of the resonator time series to check for any delayed response or slow drift emerging 10+ days post-perturbation, (2) data to test whether resonator_lab self-correlation at longer lags (14+ days) reflects genuine oscillation or random noise, and (3) a check on the hypothesis that resonators decouple or actively suppress the perturbation. If resonator_lab readings today cluster near the baseline mean (2.6980) rather than the slightly elevated post-baseline mean (2.7054), it supports genuine insensitivity. If they drift or show structure, it may revise p for the 'slow drift' or 'delayed response' hypotheses upward.

state.question: Why do independent instrument pairs (pendulum_lab vs pendulum_obs; resonator_lab vs resonator_obs) show near-zero or negative cross-correlation at multiple time offsets, when they purport to measure the same physical quantity?

hypotheses.label: Instrumental isolation / independent noise sources
hypotheses.rationale: Each instrument pair is physically separate. If pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs measure the same underlying oscillation but are decoupled mechanically and electronically, they would each pick up independent environmental noise, thermal drift, or sensor artifacts. Cross-correlation would be weak even if both tracked reality faithfully. The small sample sizes at long offsets (n=24–30) make even weak true signals hard to detect. This is the most parsimonious explanation: two working instruments, poor coupling.

hypotheses.label: Systematic measurement error in one or more instruments (e.g., drift, bias, calibration drift undetected within 10-day baseline)
hypotheses.rationale: Individual instruments show no clear level change in the baseline period, but drift would not necessarily manifest as a step. If one instrument (e.g., pendulum_lab or resonator_obs) has a slow, smooth drift in scale factor or offset over days 1–10, its readings would diverge from the others' without any visible discontinuity. The absence of self-correlation at known lags (pendulum_lab 0.348 at 6 days, resonator_lab -0.319 at 2 days) is marginally consistent with this: instruments may be drifting, reducing their own reproducibility. The value spacing (all ≥0.0001) and low exact-repetition rates are consistent with genuine measurement noise, not a sign of systematic error, but they do not rule it out.
